content: There are several reasons why you might want to rename a page, whether it is one you created or found. These include: The title contains a spelling error. The title does not adhere to the wiki's naming conventions. The scope of the article has been altered, whether reduced, expanded, or otherwise modified. In this context, the terms rename and move are synonymous, though they represent different conceptual models of the operation: Rename: This involves keeping the page but assigning it a new name. The page history is transferred to the new name, and a new page with the old name is created as a redirect to the new name. The page history of the redirect records the renaming. Move: This involves transferring the content and page history to a new page, converting the old page into a redirect, and updating the page history to reflect the renaming. The system uses the first model, marking the old page as a new page, which avoids altering the historical record (a form of historical revisionism). However, the reason for the move is only displayed in the history of the old page name. Although all pages in all namespaces have a move link, pages in the image or category namespaces cannot be moved. To rename an image, you must re-upload it with the new name and copy the image description. To rename a category, you must update all category tags and copy the editable content. How to Rename a Page To rename a page, you must be logged in. Note the following: The move button is not available in the nostalgia skin. The button is located in the quickbar, which must be enabled. Once the correct page is displayed, click the Move tab at the top of the page. You will be prompted to provide a new name for the page and given the option to move the page's associated talk page as well. It is generally safest to select yes for this option unless you have a specific reason not to. You can provide a reason for the move, similar to an edit summary. After clicking the move page button, the page will be renamed to the new title. The old title will become a redirect page, ensuring that any links to the old title will still direct users to the new page. However, double redirects (pages that redirect to the original page) will not automatically follow the new page and must be manually updated. Page Histories The move page function preserves the entire edit history of the page, both before and after the move, in one place, as if the page had always been named that way. Therefore, you should never move a page by cutting all the text from one page and pasting it into a new one. This method makes it much harder to track old revisions, notes, and attributions. If you are splitting a page into multiple topics, you may need to use the cut-and-paste method. In such cases, include a note in the new page's edit summary and talk page indicating where the text originated. The move itself will be recorded in the edit history of the page with the old title. Moving Redirect Pages A redirect page can be moved like any other page. However, this is not recommended, as it has the same negative impact on page history as copying and pasting content to a new page and making the old page a redirect. When moving a redirect page to a new name, the redirect on the old page (now pointing to the new redirect page) must be updated to avoid double redirects. This means the old page will no longer redirect to the page containing its history. The only viable strategy that respects page histories is to adapt the redirect on the page without moving it. Moving Over a Redirect If the new title already exists but is merely a redirect to the old title with no significant history, you can rename the page. This is most commonly done when renaming a page back to its original name. This works only if the redirect created during the first renaming has not been edited. The result is that the page history is preserved, but there will be no visible record of the two moves. The edit history of the page with the intermediate title will show only the latest move. To avoid losing information, copy the relevant edit line to one of the talk pages before the second move. If the second move occurs shortly after the first, this can also be done using the Recent Changes log. Undoing a Move To undo a move from Page A to Page B, simply: 1. Move Page B back to Page A. 2. List Page B (now a history-free redirect) for deletion under Moderation/Speedy Deletions. The software requires that the redirect points to the page you are moving it from. If a vandal moved Page A to Page B to Page C, you would need to: 1. Move Page C to Page B. 2. Move Page B to Page A. If Page A has been subsequently edited or the move software behaves unpredictably, only an administrator can resolve the issue by: 1. Deleting Page A (ensuring it has no useful history and adding explicit author credit on a talk page if necessary). 2. Moving Page B to Page A. 3. Deleting Page B (which should now be a history-free redirect to Page A). Move wars are highly unproductive and result in numerous unnecessary redirects, which someone will eventually need to clean up. Other Notes If the new title already exists and is not just a redirect to the old title with no history, the wiki will prevent you from renaming the page. In such cases, you must either manually merge the two pages or, if the existing page has no real content, list it for deletion to make room for the move. Redirects to redirects are not automatically followed, as this prevents infinite loops and complex linking structures. Always check the What links here tool for your page, and if there are multiple levels of redirects, update the links to point directly to the new location. However, be cautious, as your move might be reverted. Ensure there are no objections to your move by checking the talk page first. Avoid moving a page while the edit box of the corresponding talk page is open. If you save the talk page while the move is in progress, you may overwrite the redirect to the new talk page, resulting in duplicated content.
